content: The pneumococcal vaccine 13-valent has been classified as Pregnancy Category B by the FDA. A developmental and reproductive toxicity study conducted in female rabbits at a dose approximately 20 times the human dose (on a mg/kg basis) showed no evidence of impaired female fertility or harm to the fetus due to the vaccine. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Since animal reproduction studies are not always predictive of human response, this vaccine should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. In Australia, there is no guidance from the Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) regarding the use of the pneumococcal vaccine 13-valent in pregnant women. There is no FDA guidance on the use of the pneumococcal vaccine 13-valent during labor and delivery. It is unknown whether the pneumococcal vaccine 13-valent is excreted in human milk. As many drugs are excreted in human milk, caution should be exercised when administering this vaccine to nursing women. The safety and effectiveness of Prevnar 13 in children below the age of 6 weeks have not been established. Antibody responses to the pneumococcal vaccine 13-valent were lower in individuals aged 65 years and older compared to those aged 50 through 59 years. However, no overall differences in safety outcomes were observed between these age groups. There is no FDA guidance on the use of the pneumococcal vaccine 13-valent with respect to specific gender populations, racial populations, patients with renal impairment, or patients with hepatic impairment. There is no FDA guidance on the use of the pneumococcal vaccine 13-valent in women of reproductive potential or in males. There is no FDA guidance on the use of the pneumococcal vaccine 13-valent in immunocompromised patients. Individuals with certain diseases or conditions are at increased risk of pneumococcal disease. However, immunogenicity and safety data in these populations are limited. Immune responses elicited by the pneumococcal vaccine 13-valent administered on a U.S. schedule to preterm infants have not been studied. In a study involving preterm infants (<37 weeks gestational age, N=100) who received four doses of the vaccine on a non-U.S. schedule, serotype-specific IgG antibody responses after the third and fourth doses were lower compared to responses in term infants (≥37 weeks gestational age, N=100) for some serotypes. The effectiveness of the vaccine in preterm infants cannot be established from this study. In an open-label, single-arm, descriptive study, two doses of the pneumococcal vaccine 13-valent were administered six months apart to children aged ≥6 to <18 years with sickle cell disease who had previously received PPSV23 at least six months prior to enrollment. Children with a prior history of pneumococcal conjugate vaccination were excluded. For all vaccine serotypes, anti-pneumococcal opsonophagocytic activity (OPA) geometric mean antibody titers (GMTs) were higher after the first dose compared to pre-vaccination levels (N=95–131). OPA GMTs following the first and second doses were comparable. The effectiveness of the vaccine in this specific population has not been established.
